beats.text: At thirty-eight, Montaigne locked himself in a tower to do something no one had tried.
Not to argue a grand system — but simply to watch his own mind, honestly, on paper.
He contradicted himself, changed his mind, confessed his fears. He invented the personal essay.
On his ceiling he carved a motto to keep him humble: "Que sais-je?" — What do I know?
The more he examined any certainty, the more it dissolved into doubt and exception.
But for Montaigne that wasn't defeat. Doubt made him gentle, curious, hard to fool.
Real wisdom, he decided, begins the moment you stop pretending to be sure.

source_note: From the Essays, trans. Charles Cotton (public domain) — paraphrased.
